1:
Barnes and Clarke reach the same conclusion about the date by the same route: the three names at the head stand together at the head of the first epistle, and since men of that sort were rarely long in one place, the two letters followed close upon each other from the same city. Barnes admits the proof is not certain, there being no note of time or place in the letter, and rests it on three probabilities: the companions, the error grown from a misreading of the first epistle, and a hint that trouble was gathering at Corinth. He settles on late 53 or early 54. Clarke supposes the bearer of the first letter returned with an alarming report: some expected the day of judgment immediately, some had abandoned their business as inconsistent with preparing for it, and some claimed a revelation, supporting it with a pretended message from the apostle. Ellicott dates it differently: the company that sent the first letter has not broken up, and since Silvanus does not appear with Paul after the second missionary journey, this letter falls inside it.

Clarke then turns aside into a long argument taken from another writer and endorsed. Certain learned men have held that the apostles believed the end of the world would fall within their lifetime; this, he insists, is a pernicious error, since if they erred on a matter they claimed was revealed, their authority fails everywhere else. His answer is drawn from the letter in hand: Paul tells them that those who make them believe the day is at hand are deceiving them, that a great apostasy must come first, and that the man of sin must be revealed and remain a long time before he is destroyed — none of which could happen in a few years. He adds the argument about the ingathering of the Jews after the fullness of the Gentiles.

On the salutation itself the comments are brief and go different ways. Robertson notes that the address is identical with the first epistle except that our is added after Father, and that the clause naming the Father and the Lord Jesus as the source of grace, though not genuine in the earlier place, belongs here and in every other Pauline letter; he observes that Jesus Christ is set on a level with God without being identified with Him, and that the preposition of the first verse marks the sphere in which the church exists, that of the second the fountain from which grace and peace flow. Ellicott judges likewise, that the clause is wrongly added to the first epistle and stands rightly here. Calvin fastens on the word church: not merely a company gathered under the banner of faith, but the work and building of the Father as much as of Christ, since it is by God adopting and regenerating us that we come to be in Christ at all. Henry observes that the introduction repeats the former word for word, and draws a lesson: Paul did not find it grievous to write the same things twice, and ministers should regard the truth and usefulness of their doctrine more than variety of expression, lest an affectation of novelty carry them into new notions. Chrysostom takes the wish for grace as the point of the greeting: most men contrive everything to gain favour with rulers, but how much greater to find favour with God, which is why Paul opens every letter with it. He proves it from Joseph — a young slave set over a harsh master’s house, falsely accused and thrown into prison by a man too angry to notice that the one stripped of the garment was the one who had suffered violence — who, when God poured out grace on him, passed through it all as though the trials had never happened, and came at last to a throne.
3:
Ellicott takes the opening words to mean a debt actually incurred, which it would be dishonesty not to pay, and argues that the clause of reason attaches to as it is meet, since otherwise that phrase would add nothing. Robertson draws the same distinction from the two words: the obligation points to the divine side and the fitness to the human, and the idiom recurs only once more in the letter and nowhere else in Paul’s thanksgivings. Calvin explains why the letter begins here: commendation is the road to exhortation, and one has more success with those already running when their progress is not passed over. He draws two lessons. The true commendation of believers is daily growth, which should send us to examine how far we have advanced; and since Paul thanks God for the enlargement and not only for the beginning, the enlargement must also be God’s, for if it came from human power the thanksgiving would be worthless. He adds that we owe thanks not only for good done to us but for favours bestowed on our brethren, since in a body so joined what is given to one member is gain to the whole. Wesley observes that Paul wraps his praise of men inside praise of God, and Gill grounds the constancy of the thanks in the constancy of the giving.

The verb for growth attracts all of them. Clarke says it means to grow luxuriantly, like a sound tree in good soil repaying the husbandman, and stresses that this was true not of a few members but of every one. Ellicott calls it an enthusiastic word — their faith is outgrowing all bounds — and notes that faith was the very thing whose deficiencies had worried Paul when he last wrote. Robertson identifies it as one of Paul’s many compounds in over, found only here in the New Testament, and sees a tree growing above measure; the word for the abounding of their love, he adds, answers to the prayer of the earlier letter, and one scholar treats that fulfilment as evidence for the order of the two epistles. Barnes and Wesley infer from the report of growth that news had reached Paul since the first letter went out. Ellicott finds the phrase of every one of you all telling, as showing the apostles knew how each convert fared, and concludes that the frictions addressed in the earlier letter had died away.

On the glorying, Gill is careful to distinguish the object from the subject. Paul elsewhere forbids glorying in men and does not contradict himself here: he gloried not in their riches or wisdom or strength but in their graces, and in these not as their own but as instances of the grace of God. Barnes and Clarke read it as example-holding, the Thessalonians produced before other congregations as evidence of what the gospel can do; Clarke recalls the persecution they had borne and remarks that persecution never essentially injured the genuine Church of God. Robertson observes that Paul was not above praising one church to another to provoke both to good works, and that the verb for such boasting occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; he notes a manuscript reading their being held fast in tribulation rather than bearing up. Ellicott asks why the pronoun is emphatic, and answers that the writers had themselves expressed misgivings earlier; he defines the two nouns, patience meaning not meek submissiveness but heroic endurance and faith here approaching hope while keeping the sense of faithfulness; and he distinguishes tribulation, which implies no personal enmity, from persecution, an organised party working at the annoyance of the church. Calvin notices that Paul glories not in their faith and love but in their patience and faith, and makes patience the fruit and evidence of faith: nothing sustains us under trial as faith does, and impatience betrays unbelief.
5:
Everything turns on what the token is a token of. Barnes notes that the relative is supplied by the translators, lists the candidates — their patience, the persecutions, or the whole preceding sentence — and takes the last: enduring affliction rightly proves a righteous judgment is coming. He unfolds it in three steps: that the good suffer while the wicked triumph is evidence that judgment lies ahead; the present state of things is permitted so that character may be developed; and the manner in which trials are borne indicates beforehand how the case will be decided. Ellicott locates the indication not in the vitality of their faith and love but in the bare fact of their being persecuted, and warns against pressing the epithet, as though the sense were a token of the righteousness of God’s judgment; the point is only which way a fair judge was likely to decide. Clarke offers two readings and prefers the second: the persecutions may prove that God judged rightly in calling the Gentiles in, since those who enter go through much tribulation; or they may carry the maxim that the sufferings of the just and the triumphs of the wicked prove a judgment to come. Gill rejects the readings that look to the future, because the apostle is speaking of present suffering, and settles on the seeming inequality of providence itself, which has hardened wicked men and staggered righteous ones.

Calvin sets his reading against a habit of mind. The injuries innocent people endure show, as in a mirror, that God will one day judge the world; and this stands at the antipodes of the profane thought we entertain when things go well with the bad and ill with the good, that the world runs by chance and God has no hand in it. He gathers witnesses from both sides of the ancient world: the psalmist whose feet had well-nigh slipped when he saw the prosperity of the wicked, a Latin poet who said the misfortunes of the good tempt him to think there are no gods, and the tyrant who robbed a temple and took a fair wind home for proof that heaven favours sacrilege. Since God is a just judge, He will one day restore peace to those unjustly harassed and pay their oppressors what they have earned. Robertson treats the phrase as standing in apposition or as a nominative absolute and insists the judgment in view is the final one; Wesley refers the token forward to the verses that follow. Henry finds a present advantage in the sufferings: their faith tried and their patience exercised, they were improved by what they endured, and their willingness to suffer proved them Christians indeed — for religion, if it is worth anything, is worth everything.

On being counted worthy they close ranks. Henry allows a worthiness of congruity but not of condignity: sufferings no more purchase heaven than services do, but by patience under them we are made meet for the promised joy. Barnes states flatly that the words do not mean Christians earn heaven by affliction. Clarke grants a true gospel sense of the word, since a child of God who partakes of the divine nature is worthy of the kingdom, not for anything done to merit it but because he bears the image of God, which is what gives the title. Ellicott removes the question, arguing that the phrase means declared worthy and is the sentence rather than its ground, so the dispute about merit does not arise. He adds a distinction the others miss: the Thessalonians are already in the kingdom as its subjects, and what is promised is that they be counted worthy not of admission but of the kingdom itself, to inherit and reign in it — which is why they suffer not merely to win it but on its behalf.
6:
Ellicott renders the opening words as if so be it is fair, a form Paul uses when arguing from what his readers will grant, and makes it turn on conscience: a requital of this kind commends itself as fair to men, and is it likely to seem less fair to God? What is righteous for men, he says, is righteous for God. Barnes reaches the same ground by a longer road, insisting that future punishment is not arbitrary but just, and being just will certainly be inflicted: God could not threaten such a penalty unless it were right; men who make and execute penal laws cannot call wrong in God what they think right in themselves; and nothing in the difference between this world and the next changes the nature of the act. Robertson notes that the phrase means alongside God, from God’s own standpoint, which is as near to absolute right as language can come. Gill observes that what is righteous in itself is righteous in God’s sight though not always in men’s, since persecutors may suppose they do God service; and Clarke, granting that God does not generally requite in this life, says he often gives proofs of displeasure against persecutors. Wesley points to a tumult at the passover in which by some accounts thirty thousand Jews were killed, and takes it for the beginning of the sorrows Paul had spoken of. Calvin draws the consequence: if God did not defer punishments and rewards to another judgment, the government of the world would be unjust and the name of God a dead thing.

The promise of rest they take in different measures. Gill allows a temporary relaxation, instancing the peace the churches enjoyed after the death of Stephen, but prefers the rest that remains after death and at the coming of the Lord. Ellicott makes the word the opposite of the strain at which persecution held them, and says such rest waits in its fulness for the judgment day. Barnes gathers images for it — the labourer after his toil, the soldier after a march, a man racked with pain — and marks an asymmetry the others pass over: the wicked will deserve everything they suffer, but the righteous do not deserve what they receive, their admission being wholly of grace. Robertson notes that those who shared the suffering will share the release. In the words with us three find more than syntax. Ellicott takes it as fellow feeling, the writers having earned or being still in the act of earning the same rest. Barnes thinks it adds to the comfort that they will meet their teachers there, and remarks that there is no envy among those who anticipate heaven. Calvin makes it a matter of credentials: Paul does not stand in the shade instructing them how to fight in the heat of the sun, but fights himself and calls them to the same warfare.

Robertson notes that the coming is called an unveiling rather than by the usual word for the presence. Calvin will go no further: the nature of that fire, and of what materials, he leaves to persons of foolish curiosity, contenting himself with what Paul meant to teach, that Christ will strictly avenge the injuries the wicked inflict. The terror of the description, he adds, is itself consolation, since our chief grief is the suspicion that God is lightly affected by our calamities. Over the angels there is a real difference. Clarke observes that the coming to judgment is scarcely ever mentioned without them, and calls them the court or retinue of the judge. Ellicott renders the phrase as the angels of His power, those to whom it is entrusted and by whom it is administered, and says they do not attend for pomp but to execute God’s purposes; Calvin agrees, taking them for those in whom He will exercise His power.
8:
Ellicott begins by moving a comma: most critics punctuate so that the flaming fire belongs with what follows rather than with the angels, and he insists it is not the instrument of vengeance but the pictorial attribute of the divine presence, as at the bush and at Sinai. Barnes reads it as incessant lightning, absent from the parallel passage in the earlier letter; Clarke renders it thunder and lightning. Gill leaves it open between Christ, whose appearing will be sudden and visible as lightning, and angels descending in fiery forms as at the ascent of Elijah.

Over the word for vengeance there is unusual care. Ellicott says the expression is found almost nowhere else in Greek and cannot mean taking revenge, as though the Lord had conceived a grudge; it means assigning to each man the satisfaction justice requires, on another’s behalf. Barnes puts it briefly: the word means punishment, since nothing in God answers to the passion of revenge. Calvin turns this into a question of conscience — whether it is lawful to desire such vengeance — and answers that we may not desire it upon any person, being commanded to wish well to all, and that since we cannot tell who the wicked are we ought to desire the welfare of all. Most divide the clauses by the repeated article: those who do not know God being Gentiles, those who do not obey the gospel Jews. Robertson notes both were involved at Thessalonica, Jews as instigators and Gentiles as officials. Ellicott adds that the negative particle marks the ignorance and disobedience as the grounds of punishment, so only Gentiles whose ignorance was voluntary are in view. Clarke widens the second class to nominal Christians who accept the gospel as a revelation but will not take it as a rule of life.

On the everlasting destruction they are unanimous against annihilation and various in their reasons. Barnes distinguishes the word from the one used in the judgment scene and gives the ordinary sense in which health or property is destroyed: the soul is ruined for the great purposes of its being, and will not be annihilated but linger on in destruction. Clarke cannot tell what the destruction consists in, since their being continues, and calls it the eternal presence of substantial evil with the absence of all good. Robertson finds the phrase elsewhere only of a persecuting tyrant in the Maccabean books, and grants that the adjective by itself means age-long, but holds Paul means the coming age as against this one, as eternal as the New Testament knows how to make it. Gill and Wesley arrive independently at the same argument: since the enmity continues there can be no end of the sin and therefore none of the punishment. Calvin argues from the antithesis: the perpetuity of this death is proved by its being set opposite the glory of Christ, which has no end, and its severity may be measured by that glory. Ellicott takes the banishment as the whole of it, the face of the Lord being a figure from eastern courts where only honoured servants are admitted; fellowship with Christ was God’s intention for the lost as well, which is why exclusion is a positive destruction. He then concedes what none of the others will, that on this doctrine there appear to be two sets of passages whose reconciliation seems almost impossible in our present state — where Barnes had said that if eternal punishment is not taught here it could not be taught in human language at all. Chrysostom met the same evasion long before, that men hope not by leaving their sins but by persuading themselves hell is milder and temporary; he answers that Paul calls it everlasting, and that the coming will be light to some and vengeance to others.
10:
Ellicott insists the glorifying is not the purpose of the coming but its effect, and the saints at once the objects on which and the means by which the perfection of Christ is displayed: what men see is not the greatness of the men but the divine power that could exalt them. He then draws out a symmetry the others miss. The persecutors fell into two classes, and the saved answer them one for one: against those who do not know God stand the saints, against those who do not obey stand those who believed. So the profane Gentile acknowledges the glory of the God he did not know, while the disobedient Jew wonders at what obedience has won. Barnes takes the same view of the second verb after weighing whether Christ is admired by believers rather than in them, and decides the ground of the admiration is what will be seen in them; his main honour that day will not be the splendours of his coming, nor the angels, nor his power over the elements, but the church he has redeemed. He lists what will be admired — that the plan of redemption was conceived at all, that he was willing to be made flesh and die, that he defended his church through its persecutions — and adds that this honour has never yet been seen, his people having reflected his image imperfectly and been counted the offscouring of all things. Wesley says only that the glory of Christ shall shine in them.

Calvin makes it a promise of participation: Christ will not keep this glory to himself but will gather the saints into fellowship with it, and the force of the sentence lies in the contrast with a present condition in which believers labour and are counted worthless. The purpose of setting the coming before them is that they may pursue this brief journey as it were with closed eyes, their minds on a kingdom still hidden. He notices too that saints is at once explained by them that believe, which he takes to mean there is no holiness apart from faith. Gill divides the glory in two directions: Christ will appear glorious to them, coming in his own glory, in the Father’s glory conferred on him as judge, and with the glory of the angels; and he will bestow glory on them, so that the glory of the members redounds to the head. Clarke fastens on the wonder rather than the glory: much as believers now admire the Redeemer and his condescension in becoming man, all their present amazement will be nothing to what they feel when they see him in the glory he had with the Father before the world was.

The closing parenthesis gives trouble. Clarke endorses the reading which puts the participle in the past — those who have believed — on the authority of the older manuscripts, calls it undoubtedly genuine, and judges the members of the sentence to have been strangely transposed. Ellicott accepts the same past tense and explains it as looking back from the judgment day to the moment when the gospel was offered and the division began; the clause assures the Thessalonians that they are inside the number just described, and the final words are set at the end so the reader may look once more at the sight the writer’s eyes are fixed upon. Robertson asks the same question about the tense, reports the suggestion that Paul is reassuring those who accepted his preaching when he was among them, and passes on a verdict that the parenthesis is an anti-climax. Calvin turns it to the same use but with a sharper edge: because the preaching found credit among them, Christ has already enrolled them among his own, from which we learn that the promises of God are ratified in us when they gain credit with us.
11:
Henry begins with the fact of the praying: the expectation of Christ’s coming should drive us to prayer, and since without divine instruction we do not know what to ask, our prayers should be made suitable to our expectations. Gill adds that the apostles did not content themselves with telling them these things but prayed that they might be found among those in whom Christ is glorified. Ellicott shows the connective looks back to exactly that, the word meaning whereunto.

Which calling is meant divides them. Ellicott argues that the demonstrative would have been better left out, since the calling in Paul’s mind is the summons of that last day rather than the one already obeyed; they had been called and had answered, and God was calling them still, but none of that secured their proving worthy of the last decisive call — many are called, few chosen. Robertson allows the noun to mean either the beginning or the final issue and thinks both may be present, quoting the saying that whom God counts worthy He first makes worthy. Calvin puts the same difficulty and answers it the other way: God had already called them, so Paul must mean the end, which depends on perseverance; and because we are liable to give way, our calling would prove vain so far as we are concerned if God did not confirm it. Henry and Clarke read the verb as a prayer that God would first make them worthy, Henry because we have no worthiness of our own, Clarke because only continual supplies of grace enable anyone to adorn the calling.

The phrase about good pleasure produces the sharpest exchange in the chapter, though neither party names the other. Calvin says Paul rises to an amazing height in extolling grace, not content with the word for pleasure but tracing it to goodness; and if the good pleasure of God is the cause of our salvation and rests on nothing but His goodness, we are worse than mad if we ascribe to our own merits anything however small. This sets aside, he adds, the contrivance by which we are anticipated by grace and then helped along by subsequent merits, for Paul recognises in the whole progress of salvation nothing but pure grace. Clarke, on the same words, works through them in stages — that God’s own goodness called them, that it is the pleasure of that goodness to save, and that He proved it by sending His Son — and then states the condition plainly: if they are faithful to His grace He will accomplish it, for though the power must come from Him, the exercise of that power must be of themselves. Ellicott declines the reading most modern commentators take, that the goodness is the Thessalonians’ own and the clause a prayer that their aspirations be fulfilled; he takes beneficence almost as a personified abstraction, so that God will accomplish upon them everything beneficence can devise. Robertson notes that the first noun means more than desire and turns the phrase into a wish that they find delight in goodness. Wesley defines it as perfect holiness, and Henry says that if there is any good in us it is the fruit of God’s good will, which is why it is called grace.

The closing phrase they refer to God rather than to the readers. Ellicott is explicit that the work is God’s and not the Thessalonians’, the sense being not to perfect their faithful activity but to bring to consummation what faith was able to effect in them, faith being opposed here as much to sight as to unbelief. Calvin reads it the same way, as the completing of a building God began, and finds the words about power significant because perfecting faith is a matter of the greatest difficulty. Barnes glosses the power as effectual and complete.
12:
Robertson raises the hardest question in the verse and declines to settle it. Because a single article governs both nouns at the close, strict syntax requires that one person be meant, as it plainly does in two other well known passages, so that Paul would be calling Jesus Christ our God and Lord. But the argument is weakened because the word for Lord is often used as a proper name without the article, which is not true of the corresponding word in those passages; so Robertson admits Paul may mean the grace of our God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, or equally the grace of our God and Lord, Jesus Christ. Calvin knows the question is there and steps round it, saying it is unnecessary to explain here in what sense the glory belongs to God and Christ in common. Ellicott takes a smaller decision about the same clause, holding that the words about grace attach only to the glorifying of the readers in Christ, not of Christ in them, and that grace here scarcely bears its strict theological sense.

On the mutual glorifying they are close together. Robertson calls the reciprocity Pauline and likens it to the vine and the branches. Calvin says the goodness of God shines out first in this, that He makes His glory conspicuous in people covered with ignominy, and the miracle is doubled when He afterwards irradiates them with that glory as though in return; yet nothing in it is ours, since only by the Spirit is a life made to contribute to God’s glory. Ellicott reads the verse as gathering up the preceding paragraph: in that day the lost as well as the saved must acknowledge the perfection of the Jesus whose Christship they rejected and the dignity of the Christians they despised, and the two recognitions are one act, since to acknowledge what He is concedes that His followers were right. Gill observes that the name of Christ is dishonoured by the unworthy walk of professors and glorified by their faith and patience, and adds that if the work were not completed in them Christ would lose the glory of their redemption. Clarke makes it the end of the calling that Jesus should have his passion magnified in the life of those he died for, and finds in the last clause a rule: God saves as it becomes God to save. Wesley says the love and power of the Lord are to be displayed in them; Barnes glosses the name as standing for the person and reads the second half as a wish that they be owned as His friends when He comes to judge.

Both Barnes and Clarke close the chapter with a charge rather than an exposition. Barnes reviews what he takes the chapter to have established: that the wicked will certainly be punished at the coming of the Lord Jesus, so plainly that if it is not so then language has no meaning; that the punishment will be eternal, since clearer words could not be chosen unless God meant to trifle with men; and that it will aggravate the suffering immeasurably that it is a righteous thing, for a man bears pain far more easily while conscience tells him he is wronged, and the lost will never have that consolation. Clarke draws two lessons of his own. The first is about human nature: persecution is aimed at people who have done the persecutor no harm and can do him none, so it proceeds from nothing but the absence of the Spirit of Christ — and men may amuse themselves arguing against original sin, but while religious persecution exists their arguments are disproved absolutely. The second is about the pulpit: the everlasting destruction of the ungodly ought to be kept continually before men, since no one takes measures to escape a danger he is not convinced exists.
